title: Next-Token Prediction — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Predicting and Generating Tokens in Large Language Models · Subject: Transformers and LLM Architecture. Three beginner, two medium, two advanced questions with distinct visual explanations.
hero:
NEXT-TOKEN PREDICTION · VISUAL OVERVIEW

An LLM builds text one token at a time

Given the tokens already available, a decoder model estimates which token could come next, selects one, appends it, and repeats. Tokens are not always complete words.

questions.stem: What is Next-Token Prediction in Large Language Models (LLMs), and how does it enable models like GPT to generate text by predicting one token at a time?
questions.tag: Beginner · one token at a time
options: Next-token prediction generates an entire answer all at once, without calculating which token should follow the sequence the model has already seen.
Next-token prediction uses the preceding tokens to estimate one continuation at a time, adding chosen tokens to produce longer generated text.
Next-token prediction searches training records for an exact completed response, then copies it without evaluating new token probabilities for the current prompt.
Next-token prediction converts words to numbers but never uses those numbers to generate more language after reading the user's original prompt.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine an AI helping a gardener write labels for seed packets. After “Plant the seeds in,” the model scores possible next tokens such as “spring” or “soil.” It selects one and uses the longer phrase to make the next prediction. Repeating this process can produce a complete instruction. Next-token prediction is a training objective and a generation mechanism used by GPT-style models. It is not the same as copying a stored answer or creating every word simultaneously.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. Next-token prediction means learning a conditional distribution over the next token given the previous tokens, p(x_t | x_1,...,x_{t-1}). Decoder-only language models such as GPT tokenize a prompt, process it through masked self-attention, and produce vocabulary logits. A decoding strategy selects a new token, which is appended and used as context for the following prediction. This autoregressive loop continues until an end-of-sequence token, a maximum length, or another stopping condition is reached. The model does not normally plan every word of its full answer in a single forward pass.
questions.figure:
01 · Beginner · main idea

Predict a token, add it, and predict again

Easy idea: An LLM continues text by repeatedly predicting the next token using the sequence generated so far.

questions.stem: What exactly is a token, and how does an LLM decide what might come next when it receives a sentence such as "The cat is sitting on the"?
options: A token must be one complete English word, so the model chooses the next word simply by sorting its vocabulary in alphabetical order.
A token is only punctuation; written words are processed by a separate unrelated system, so language prediction never uses word or subword pieces.
A token can be a word, subword, or punctuation piece; the model uses earlier token context to score what might come next.
A token always represents an entire finished sentence, so the model cannot use smaller pieces to construct longer replies step by step.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Picture a message ending with “The cat is sitting on the.” A model might predict “mat,” but it makes this choice using tokens, which are pieces defined by its tokenizer. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, or punctuation; it is not always one English word. The model assigns scores to possible next pieces based on earlier context. The selected piece is then added to the sequence, which influences following choices.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: C. A token is an element of the tokenizer's vocabulary. Depending on the tokenizer and language, tokens may correspond to a word, whitespace-prefixed word, subword fragment, punctuation, or other text piece. For The cat is sitting on the, the tokenizer converts text into token IDs. The decoder uses these IDs, positions, and prior context to compute logits for all possible next token IDs. Softmax converts logits into probabilities. The illustrated mat, floor, and sofa probabilities are hypothetical, not actual outputs from GPT.
questions.figure:
02 · Beginner · what is a token?

A token may be a word, a word piece, or punctuation

Easy idea: What comes next depends on the previous tokens; a token does not have to be a complete word.

questions.stem: How does an LLM generate a complete sentence using Next-Token Prediction, starting with an input prompt, predicting the first new token, adding it to the existing sequence, and repeating the process until generation stops?
options: The model predicts a token, appends it to the running sequence, and repeats with updated context until it reaches a stopping condition.
The model chooses the last word first, then fills earlier gaps by reading future tokens that have already been generated for the full answer.
The model creates one giant answer token and later divides it into words, instead of estimating successive token probabilities while writing.
The model appends unrelated random vocabulary items without checking the expanded context again, so its later selections cannot build on earlier words.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Suppose an assistant writes directions for setting up a camera tripod. It receives a prompt, calculates probabilities for the next token, and chooses one. That token joins the sequence, so the next prediction sees the instructions written so far. The loop continues until the model produces a stop token or reaches a configured limit. The result grows one token at a time. It does not plan an entire reply by filling in already written future words.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. Autoregressive inference begins by tokenizing the prompt and computing a next-token distribution. The model selects a token according to a chosen strategy (for example greedy search or sampling), adds that token ID to the current sequence, and repeats. A sample continuation of The sun could be rises, then in, then the, then east, followed by an end token. Real token boundaries may differ from the illustrated words. Generation can stop at an EOS token, maximum new token count, or configured stop sequence. A KV cache can avoid recomputing previously processed attention Keys and Values on every step.
questions.figure:
03 · Beginner · complete sentence

The newly generated token becomes part of the next prompt

Easy idea: Generation continues until an end-of-sequence token or another stopping rule, such as a length limit.

questions.stem: How does a decoder-only Transformer calculate the probability of the next token using token embeddings, positional information, causal self-attention, hidden states, output logits, and the Softmax function?
options: Next-token probabilities come entirely from the numerical positions of tokens, without using contextual embeddings, attention, or learned hidden representations.
The model generates a complete answer first, then assigns scores to each token after the words are already chosen, making the probabilities irrelevant.
Softmax creates embeddings from raw vocabulary IDs, then passes them backward into attention before the model processes the original prompt.
Embeddings and position information enter causal decoder blocks; final hidden states produce vocabulary logits that Softmax turns into next-token probabilities.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine a model continuing a short weather forecast. First, token embeddings represent the input, and positional information shows order. Decoder blocks use causal self-attention so each position can read only earlier permitted tokens. The final hidden state feeds an output projection that produces a logit for each vocabulary token. Softmax converts those scores into probabilities. A decoding method then selects a token to continue the forecast. Each stage has a separate job in this pipeline.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: D. An LLM first embeds input token IDs and incorporates positional information. Decoder layers use causally masked self-attention and feed-forward networks to form context-sensitive hidden states. The last position's hidden state is projected by an output head to vocabulary logits, optionally with tied embedding weights. After any chosen logit transformations (such as temperature, repetition penalties, or filtering), Softmax provides a probability distribution across next-token IDs. The causal mask prevents current positions from accessing future tokens. This gives a conditional distribution, not a guarantee that the most probable word is factual or desirable.
questions.figure:
04 · Medium · decoder pipeline

Embeddings → masked attention → hidden state → logits → probabilities

Easy idea: The decoder creates a hidden representation of the context, then scores possible next tokens using logits and Softmax.

Next-token distribution: p(next token | preceding tokens) = softmax(logits at final position). Each output logit scores a vocabulary token. Numerical probabilities depend on the model and prompt.

questions.stem: How do Greedy Decoding, Temperature Sampling, Top-K Sampling, and Top-P (Nucleus) Sampling affect the selection of the next token, and why can the same prompt produce different responses even when the underlying probability distribution is similar?
options: Greedy decoding changes the model's weights while generating, and Top-k permanently removes vocabulary entries even after the current request finishes.
Greedy chooses the highest score; temperature changes probability sharpness; Top-k keeps leading candidates and Top-p keeps a probability-mass group.
Temperature directly fixes the number of tokens in the final response, while Top-p makes every chosen word repeat the same token.
Top-k always selects the rarest tokens, while Top-p always chooses the highest-scoring word regardless of how its candidates are sampled.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Picture a game narrator deciding how to finish “The door slowly …” The model assigns probabilities to possible continuations. Greedy decoding always picks the highest one. Lower temperature usually concentrates the distribution, while higher temperature makes more options plausible. Top-k limits sampling to a fixed number of leading tokens; Top-p uses a probability-mass threshold. Because sampling introduces randomness, the same prompt can produce different stories even with unchanged model weights.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. Greedy decoding deterministically chooses the highest-probability next token. Sampling selects randomly according to a distribution, and different random samples may produce different outputs. Temperature T>0 divides logits by T before Softmax; lower T makes probabilities sharper and higher T flatter. Top-K keeps the K highest-scoring tokens. Top-P (nucleus) sampling keeps the smallest probability-ranked prefix whose cumulative mass is at least p. After filtering, allowed probabilities are renormalized and sampled. Methods can be combined, and actual output may vary because different choices lead to different subsequent contexts. The shown token choices and bar heights are illustrative.
questions.figure:
05 · Medium · decoding choices

Decoding settings change the choice, even with similar model scores

Easy idea: Greedy always chooses the top candidate; sampling methods reshape or narrow choices, then draw from their remaining chances.

Sampling detail: Temperature rescales logits before Softmax. Top-K keeps the K highest-scoring tokens, while Top-P keeps the smallest probability-ranked set whose cumulative mass reaches the threshold, then renormalizes. These settings may be combined; no sampling outcome is guaranteed.

questions.stem: How is a Large Language Model trained for Next-Token Prediction using shifted input-target sequences, causal masking, cross-entropy loss, teacher forcing, and backpropagation, and how does this training differ from autoregressive inference?
options: Training uses only the model's own generated guesses, without access to actual next-token labels or any error signal for improving parameters.
Shifted targets are copies of the current input positions, and causal masking reveals future words so the model can use the correct answer directly.
Training uses real next-token targets, causal masks, cross-entropy, and backpropagation; inference instead feeds generated tokens back into future predictions.
Backpropagation begins only after generating a user-facing reply, rather than during learning from many labeled next-token examples in the training dataset.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Suppose a model learns from thousands of short cooking instructions. During training, each input position has a known next token, creating shifted targets. A causal mask stops attention from reading later target positions. Cross-entropy measures prediction error, and backpropagation updates the model's parameters. Teacher forcing uses the true earlier tokens for these training predictions. During inference, the model must use its own generated continuations, so a poor token can influence everything that follows.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: C. In causal language-model training, a token sequence x_1,...,x_n is used with next-token targets shifted one position, so at position i the model predicts x_{i+1}. Ground-truth preceding tokens are supplied (teacher forcing), and a causal mask blocks access to future input positions. Although generation is sequential, training can calculate next-token predictions for many positions in parallel and average cross-entropy loss, then update model parameters using backpropagation and an optimizer. During autoregressive inference, model weights are normally fixed, gold next-token targets are unavailable, and newly generated tokens become subsequent context. Training targets may include EOS and special control tokens.
questions.figure:
06 · Advanced · training vs generation

Training has correct next-token targets; inference must use its guesses

Easy idea: Teacher forcing uses true preceding tokens during training; generation repeatedly conditions on whatever tokens the model has produced.

Parallel training: With shifted targets, positions can be scored together under a causal mask, and cross-entropy gradients update weights through backpropagation. Inference: future ground-truth tokens are unavailable, so tokens are chosen autoregressively and appended one step at a time.

questions.stem: What architectural and computational challenges arise when performing Next-Token Prediction in production LLMs, including long-context processing, KV caching, prefill versus decode phases, memory bandwidth limitations, and inference latency, and how do techniques such as speculative decoding and efficient attention improve generation performance?
options: Prefill processes the prompt, KV caching reuses earlier Keys and Values, decode generates tokens, and speculative methods verify proposed draft continuations.
KV caching stores only old Query vectors, forcing the model to rebuild all earlier Key and Value projections whenever it generates another token.
Prefill produces the entire answer instantly, while decode repeatedly tokenizes the original prompt without generating any additional output tokens.
Speculative decoding always changes the target model's answer distribution and guarantees lower latency for every request, regardless of model size or workload.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine an online writing assistant serving many people with long drafts. During prefill, the model processes the incoming prompt; during decode, it generates further tokens. A KV cache keeps earlier Keys and Values for reuse, reducing repeated work. Long contexts still consume memory and bandwidth. Speculative decoding can verify proposals from a faster model to improve throughput or latency. Teams measure these benefits because an optimization is not equally useful for every workload.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. During prefill, the model processes the prompt and computes per-layer Key/Value states, commonly in parallel across positions subject to causal attention. Decode then produces new tokens sequentially, reading past KV tensors from cache and appending current K/V rather than recomputing all previous states. Long contexts enlarge KV-cache storage and memory-bandwidth demands; token generation can be memory-bandwidth-limited, particularly at low batch sizes. Efficient attention algorithms and KV-cache layouts reduce traffic or memory overhead. Speculative decoding lets a fast draft model suggest multiple tokens; the larger target verifies them, potentially accepting several at once. Proper speculative sampling can preserve the target model's token distribution, but speedups depend on acceptance rates, overhead, and hardware. Latency and throughput should both be measured.
questions.figure:
07 · Advanced · inference engineering

Cache past attention information and reduce expensive sequential work

Easy idea: KV caching avoids recomputing past Keys and Values, while speculative decoding can reduce the number of expensive serial steps.

Production insight: Prefill processes prompt positions and constructs per-layer KV state. Decode typically generates one token per model step while reusing past Keys/Values. Long contexts increase cache memory and bandwidth costs. Efficient attention improves memory traffic; speculative decoding uses cheaper draft tokens and a target verifier, with speedups depending on acceptance rates and implementation. The original exact speculative sampling algorithm preserves the target distribution.
